terms.definition: A family of methods that estimates a system of relationships among constructs together with the measurement of those constructs by observed indicators.
A reasoned explanation of why constructs are related. In SEM it is the source of the hypotheses and of the direction of every arrow; estimation cannot supply it.
A testable statement derived from theory, such as "perceived usefulness positively influences intention". In a path diagram each structural hypothesis is one directed arrow.
A drawing of a model: constructs as ovals, indicators as rectangles, measurement and structural relationships as arrows, covariances as two-headed arrows.
A concept that cannot be observed directly, such as satisfaction or perceived usefulness, and is measured through indicators.
The variable that represents a construct in a model. In CB-SEM it is a common factor; in PLS-SEM it is approximated by a weighted composite of indicators.
An observed variable, usually a questionnaire item, that measures a construct. In SEM Studio each indicator is bound to a data column.
The set of values an indicator can take, given by the response format (for example 1–7 agreement). Its endpoints belong to the instrument, not to the sample.
A rating item with ordered response categories, such as 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. Items with five or more roughly symmetric categories are often analysed as continuous.
The lowest and highest permissible values of an indicator's response scale, such as 1 and 7. Needed for reverse scoring and IPMA; never replaced by the observed minimum and maximum.
The part of a model that links each construct to its indicators (reflective or formative). In PLS-SEM it is called the outer model.
The part of a model that links constructs to each other with directed paths. In PLS-SEM it is called the inner model.
A construct that receives no structural arrow; the model does not explain it.
A construct that receives at least one structural arrow; it has an R² and a disturbance.
The average product of two variables' deviations from their means; positive when they tend to move together. Its size depends on the variables' units.
Covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations; unit-free, between −1 and 1, and symmetric.
The part of an indicator not due to its construct: random noise plus item-specific variance. Random error attenuates relationships between observed scores.
The difference between an observed value and the value a model implies, for a case, a variance or a covariance.
The unexplained part of an endogenous construct, collecting all causes not in the model; its variance is 1 − R² in standardised terms.
The share of an observed score's variance that is not random measurement error.
The degree to which a measure captures the construct it is intended to measure; assessed through content, convergent and discriminant validity, among others.
Factor analysis in which every item may load on every factor, used to discover a measurement structure from data.
Factor analysis in which the analyst specifies in advance which indicators load on which factor; the omitted loadings are testable constraints.
Different models that imply the same covariance matrix and therefore fit any data equally well, such as X → Y and Y → X in a two-variable model.
Drawing conclusions about cause and effect. In SEM, causal interpretation rests on theory and design (temporal order, experiments, ruling out confounders), not on estimates or fit.
SEM in which constructs are estimated as weighted composites of their indicators by an iterative algorithm, with paths estimated by OLS on the composite scores.
SEM in which constructs are common factors and parameters are chosen so that the model-implied covariance matrix reproduces the observed one, usually by maximum likelihood.
A construct represented as an exact weighted sum of its indicators. It contains everything in the indicators, including their measurement error.
A construct represented as the shared cause of its indicators; each indicator is the factor times a loading plus a unique error.
A measurement model in which the construct causes its indicators: items are interchangeable, should correlate highly, and dropping one does not change the construct's meaning.
A measurement model in which the indicators form the construct: they need not correlate, and dropping one changes the construct's meaning. In SEM Studio such blocks are declared composite-formative.
PLS outer-weight estimation in which each weight is proportional to the correlation between the indicator and the construct's inner proxy. Used for reflective blocks.
PLS outer-weight estimation in which the inner proxy is regressed on all of a block's indicators jointly; weights are multiple-regression coefficients and are sensitive to collinearity.
An indicator's coefficient in the weighted sum that forms its construct score; the main result for composite constructs.
The correlation between an indicator and its construct score (PLS), or the coefficient of the factor in the indicator's equation (CB-SEM, standardised).

The rule PLS uses to build a construct's inner proxy from its neighbours: centroid (signs of correlations), factorial (correlations) or path weighting (regression for predecessors, correlation for successors).
The estimated effect of one construct on another in the structural model: a partial regression coefficient, usually standardised.
A coefficient in standard-deviation units: the expected change in SDs of the outcome per SD of the predictor, holding other predictors constant.
A coefficient in the original units of the variables; IPMA importance is an unstandardised total effect on the rescaled 0–100 scores.
The fact that a construct's sign is arbitrary: reversing all its weights or loadings gives an equally valid solution. Software orients blocks by a convention.
Transforming a negatively worded item so that high values mean the same as for the other items: x′ = (min + max) − x, with the scale endpoints.
A correction of PLS (Dijkstra & Henseler 2015) that uses ρA to disattenuate correlations among reflective constructs, so that they are estimated as common factors. Composites are left unchanged.
The weakening of correlations and regression coefficients between scores that contain random measurement error.
A convergent-validity check for a formative construct: its correlation with an alternative (often single-item, reflective) measure of the same concept. SEM Studio does not run it automatically yet.
The extent to which the indicators cover the full domain of the construct as defined; established by definition and expert judgement before data analysis.
The share of an indicator's variance explained by its construct: the squared standardised loading, λ².
An internal-consistency reliability coefficient for reflective scales that assumes equal loadings; with unequal loadings it tends to underestimate reliability.
A reliability coefficient for reflective constructs in PLS (Dijkstra & Henseler 2015), typically between α and ρC; used by PLSc for the consistency correction.
A reliability coefficient computed from the loadings: (Σλ)² / ((Σλ)² + Σ(1 − λ²)). With classic PLS loadings it tends to overstate reliability.
The mean of the squared standardised loadings of a reflective construct's indicators; .50 or more is the usual heuristic for convergent validity.
Evidence that the indicators of a construct measure the same thing: for reflective constructs AVE, for formative ones redundancy analysis.
Evidence that a construct is empirically distinct from other constructs; assessed mainly with HTMT or HTMT2.

The mean correlation between indicators of two different constructs divided by the geometric mean of their mean within-construct correlations; estimates the construct correlation (Henseler et al. 2015).
A variant of HTMT that uses geometric instead of arithmetic means of correlations and remains consistent when loadings differ within a construct (Roemer et al. 2021).
The requirement that each construct's AVE exceeds its squared correlations with other constructs. It often fails to detect discriminant-validity problems (Henseler et al. 2015).
Correlations of an indicator with constructs other than its own; an indicator should correlate more with its own construct. A weak criterion for discriminant validity on its own.
1 / (1 − R²ⱼ), where R²ⱼ comes from regressing predictor j on the other predictors. Measures collinearity among predictor constructs or Mode B indicators.
Strong overlap among predictors, which makes their separate effects hard to estimate, inflates standard errors and can flip signs.
The share of an endogenous construct's variance explained by its predictors in the estimation sample.
R² corrected for the number of predictors relative to the sample size, so that adding useless predictors does not raise it automatically.
The change in R² when a predictor is omitted, divided by 1 − R² of the full model; .02, .15 and .35 are Cohen's small, medium and large.
The effect of one construct on another along their direct path, holding the other predictors constant.
An effect transmitted through one or more mediators; along a route it equals the product of the path coefficients.
The indirect effect along one particular route through specified mediators.
The direct effect plus all indirect effects of one construct on another.
An effect of X on Y that runs, at least partly, through a mediator M. Tested through the indirect effect with a bootstrap interval and classified with the Zhao et al. (2010) typology.
A situation in which the strength of an effect depends on a third variable; modelled with an interaction term or a multigroup analysis. SEM Studio does not estimate interactions yet.
The root mean square of the differences between observed and model-implied correlations. Used in CB-SEM and, with different properties, in PLS-SEM.
A resampling method: draw many samples with replacement from the data, re-estimate on each, and use the distribution of the estimates for standard errors and intervals.
The standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples; with the bootstrap, the SD of the resampled estimates.
A range of values for a parameter produced by a procedure that covers the true value in a stated share (e.g. 95%) of repeated samples.
A bootstrap confidence interval whose limits are percentiles of the bootstrap estimates, e.g. the 2.5th and 97.5th for 95%.
A bootstrap interval that adjusts the percentiles for bias and skewness of the bootstrap distribution. Not yet available in SEM Studio.
The starting value of a random-number generator; with the same seed, data and settings, a bootstrap draws exactly the same resamples.

The probability, under the null hypothesis and the model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. Not the probability that the hypothesis is true, and not a measure of effect size.
Comparing model parameters between groups with a formal test of the differences. Not yet available in SEM Studio.
Evidence that constructs are measured the same way across groups; required before comparing paths or means (configural, metric, scalar levels in CB-SEM; MICOM for composites).
A three-step procedure for composites: configural invariance, compositional invariance, and equality of composite means and variances (Henseler et al. 2016). Not yet available in SEM Studio.
How well a model reproduces or explains the data used to estimate it, e.g. R². Optimistic about new data.
How well a model estimated on training data predicts cases it has not seen, assessed by cross-validation or a hold-out sample.
A k-fold cross-validation procedure for PLS-SEM that reports Q²predict and compares prediction errors with a linear-model benchmark (Shmueli et al. 2016, 2019). Not yet available in SEM Studio.
A significance test of whether a model's out-of-sample prediction loss differs from a benchmark's or another model's (Liengaard et al. 2021). Not yet available in SEM Studio.
Information from evaluation cases influencing model building, for example by selecting items on the full sample before cross-validation; it makes out-of-sample results optimistic.
A map of each predecessor of a target construct by importance (unstandardised total effect) and performance (mean score rescaled to 0–100 with the scale endpoints).
In IPMA, the unstandardised total effect of a construct on the target construct, computed on the rescaled scores; it keeps its sign.
In IPMA, the mean of a construct or indicator rescaled to 0–100 with the declared scale endpoints: (x̄ − min) / (max − min) × 100.
The property that a model's parameters can be determined uniquely from the variances and covariances of the indicators. Necessary: no more free parameters than distinct moments.
In CB-SEM, the number of distinct variances and covariances minus the number of free parameters; df > 0 makes global fit testable.
An identification method that fixes one loading of each factor to 1, giving the factor the scale of that indicator.
An identification method that fixes each exogenous factor's variance to 1. Fit and standardised results equal those of marker identification.
The default CB-SEM estimator: chooses parameters that maximise the likelihood under multivariate normality.
ML estimates with robust (sandwich) standard errors and a scaled test statistic, for non-normal continuous data.
An estimator for ordinal indicators that fits polychoric correlations with a diagonal weight matrix and robust corrections. Available in lavaan, not in SEM Studio's browser engine.
ML estimation that uses every observed value of every case, unbiased when data are missing at random. Available for CB-SEM in SEM Studio, with a mean structure.
Dropping every case that has any missing value. Unbiased only if data are missing completely at random, and wasteful.
The process that produced missing values: missing completely at random (MCAR), at random given observed data (MAR), or not at random (MNAR).
A test of whether the model reproduces the population covariances exactly; sensitive to sample size.

aliases: root mean square error of approximation
terms.definition: Misfit per degree of freedom: √(max(χ² − df, 0) / (df · N)) in lavaan's convention. Near 0 means close fit.
Improvement in fit relative to a baseline model of uncorrelated indicators: 1 − max(χ² − df, 0) / max(χ²_B − df_B, χ² − df, 0).
An incremental fit index that compares χ²/df of the model and of the baseline model, penalising complexity.
How closely the model-implied covariances reproduce the observed ones. Good fit is necessary but not sufficient for a model to be correct.
A covariance or correlation residual (observed minus implied) on a standardised scale; large values show where a model fails.
The expected drop in χ² if one fixed parameter were freed. A diagnostic suggestion, never a reason to change a model on its own. Not yet available in SEM Studio.
A negative variance estimate (and a standardised loading above 1), which makes a solution inadmissible.
Obtaining the same results from the same model, data, settings, seed and code.
Whether an effect is large enough to matter in context, judged from its size and interval rather than its p value.
Variance shared by measures because of the measurement method (e.g. one questionnaire, one respondent) rather than the constructs; it can inflate relationships.
